title: Statistical quality control from Shewhart control charts to acceptance sampling
pressure: Mass production created variation at scales where inspecting every finished unit was costly and where a defect count alone did not distinguish a stable process from a process whose generating conditions had changed.
preExistingWorldModel: Industrial inspection existed, and statistics had matured in other sciences. Bell Telephone Laboratories faced high-volume manufacturing/reliability problems and needed methods that acted on the process rather than merely sorting output after production.
candidateRoutes: Shewhart control-chart monitoring of process variation
operator/engineering intervention when process signals leave expected variation
observationsAndInstruments: Shewhart issued a May 16, 1924 Bell Labs memorandum containing the sketch of a modern control chart.
The method separated variation expected from a stable process from signals associated with assignable/special causes.
Dodge and Romig developed statistical sampling inspection at Bell Labs, adding a different cost/risk tradeoff from continuous process monitoring.
decisiveTests: A useful chart had to identify changes early enough to alter production rather than merely describe history.
Sampling plans had to trade inspection burden against risks to producer and consumer.
A stable-looking metric could not substitute for checking whether process conditions remained comparable.
technicalOrScientificTransition: Quality shifted from final-product sorting toward statistical observation of the production process and decision rules tied to variation regimes.
rivalsAndFailures: Inspection can detect bad units without improving the generating process.
Overly tight limits create excessive intervention; overly loose limits miss real shifts.
A chart calibrated on one process/product cannot be assumed valid under changed conditions.
diffusionAndScaling: Control charts and acceptance sampling became reusable industrial methods and later wartime/postwar quality infrastructures rather than one Bell product.
standardsAndInstitutions: Bell Labs, industrial quality organizations, standards and training translated statistical ideas into repeatable operating practice.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Quality optimization can externalize cost to suppliers/workers or optimize measured defects while missing reliability/safety dimensions outside the measured specification.
secondOrderEffects: The work lowered the cost of learning from ongoing production and made production itself a persistent experiment/observation surface.
sourceNativeSummary: Shewhart did not invent statistics or inspection; the important transition was binding statistical representation to process intervention under industrial repetition, with sampling and process control remaining distinct tools.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: How much early industrial advantage came from the chart mathematics versus measurement discipline and managerial willingness to intervene?
Which wartime diffusion claims can be cleanly separated from later Deming/Juran institutionalization?
